title: Intermediate grammar
summary: Passives, reported speech, conditionals, clauses and punctuation.

lessons.title: Active and passive voice
lessons.explain: In the active voice the subject does the action: The chef cooked the meal. In the passive voice the subject receives the action: The meal was cooked by the chef. Use the passive when the doer is unknown, unimportant or obvious. Form it with be + past participle.
structures: Present simple passive: am/is/are + past participle: English is spoken here.
Past simple passive: was/were + past participle: The window was broken.
Perfect and modal passive: has been done, can be done.
positive: The bridge was built in 1990.
Rice is grown in many countries.
The report has been sent.
negative: The window was not broken by me.
The shop is not opened on Sundays.
questions: When was the bridge built?
Is English spoken in your office?
reallife: Notices: Smoking is not allowed here.
News: Two people were rescued from the river.

mistakes.wrong: The letter was wrote yesterday.
mistakes.right: The letter was written yesterday.
mistakes.why: Use the past participle after was: written.

mistakes.wrong: The house built in 1950.
mistakes.right: The house was built in 1950.
mistakes.why: The passive needs a form of be.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is passive?
options: The teacher marked the tests.
The tests were marked by the teacher.
The teacher is marking the tests.

exercises.prompt: The cake ___ made by my mother. (was / were)
exercises.why: The cake is singular and the sentence is past.

exercises.prompt: These cars are ___ in Germany. (make)
exercises.why: Past participle of make is made.

options: The office is cleaned every day.

The thief was catch by the police.
The thief caught by the police.

assessment.prompt: English ___ spoken all over the world. (is / are)
When do we often use the passive?
options: When the doer is unknown or not important
Only in questions
Only with the future
assessment.why: The passive focuses on the action or the receiver.
Sent is the past participle of send.

lessons.title: Direct and indirect speech
lessons.explain: Direct speech repeats the exact words in quotation marks. Indirect (reported) speech tells what someone said without quoting. Usually the tense moves one step back (present to past), pronouns change, and time words change (tomorrow becomes the next day).
structures: Direct: He said, "I am tired." → Indirect: He said (that) he was tired.
Present simple → past simple; will → would; can → could.
Questions: She asked, "Where do you live?" → She asked where I lived.
positive: She said that she was busy.
He told me that he would call later.
They said they had finished.
negative: He said that he did not know.
She told us not to wait.
questions: He asked me where I worked.
She asked if I was ready.
reallife: Passing on a message: Ravi said he would be late.
Reporting a meeting: The manager said that sales had increased.

mistakes.wrong: She asked me where do I live.
mistakes.right: She asked me where I lived.
mistakes.why: In reported questions use normal statement order, with no do.

mistakes.wrong: He told that he was tired.
mistakes.right: He said that he was tired. / He told me that he was tired.
mistakes.why: Tell needs an object (told me). Say does not.

exercises.prompt: Report: 'I am hungry,' she said.
options: She said she is hungry now.
She said she was hungry.
She said she were hungry.
exercises.why: Present simple moves back to past simple.

exercises.prompt: 'I will call you,' he said. → He said he ___ call me. (will / would)

options: He asked me where I lived.

options: He said he can swim.

options: She asked if I was ready.
She asked was I ready.

assessment.why: Use if with yes/no questions and statement order.

assessment.why: Tomorrow changes to the next day.

options: He told me to be quiet.
He told to me be quiet.
He said me to be quiet.

lessons.title: Conditional sentences
lessons.explain: Conditionals have an if-clause and a result clause. Zero conditional is for facts (if + present, present). First conditional is for real future possibilities (if + present, will + base verb). Second conditional is for unreal or unlikely situations (if + past, would + base verb).
structures: Zero: If you heat ice, it melts.
First: If it rains, we will stay home.
Second: If I had more time, I would learn Spanish.
positive: If you study, you will pass.
If I won the lottery, I would travel the world.
If you mix red and blue, you get purple.
negative: If it does not rain, we will go out.
If I were you, I would not buy it.
questions: What will you do if you miss the bus?
What would you do if you were rich?
reallife: Making a plan: If the weather is good, we will have a picnic.
Giving advice: If I were you, I would talk to your manager.

mistakes.wrong: If it will rain, we will stay home.
mistakes.right: If it rains, we will stay home.
mistakes.why: Do not use will in the if-clause.

mistakes.wrong: If I would have more money, I would buy it.
mistakes.right: If I had more money, I would buy it.
mistakes.why: In the second conditional, use the past simple in the if-clause.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct first conditional.
options: If it rains, we will stay in.
If it will rain, we stay in.
If it rained, we will stay in.
exercises.why: If + present simple, will + base verb.

exercises.prompt: If I ___ rich, I would buy a boat. (be)
exercises.why: Second conditional uses the past: were (or was).

exercises.prompt: Which sentence states a general fact?
options: If you heat water to 100 degrees, it boils.

options: If I had wings, I would fly.

options: If I lived near the sea, I would swim every day.
If I would live near the sea, I swim every day.
If I live near the sea, I would swimming every day.
assessment.why: If + past simple, would + base verb.

lessons.title: Gerunds
lessons.explain: A gerund is the -ing form of a verb used as a noun. It can be a subject (Swimming is fun), an object (I enjoy swimming) or follow a preposition (She is good at swimming). Some verbs are followed by gerunds: enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest, keep.
structures: Subject: Reading helps you learn.
After verbs: enjoy, avoid, mind, finish, suggest + verb-ing.
After prepositions: good at, interested in, thinking of + verb-ing.
positive: I enjoy cooking.
She is interested in learning Japanese.
Walking is good for you.
negative: I do not mind waiting.
He avoids eating sugar.
questions: Do you enjoy dancing?
Would you mind opening the window?
reallife: Polite request: Would you mind closing the door?
Talking about hobbies: I love painting and I am good at drawing.

mistakes.wrong: I enjoy to swim.
mistakes.right: I enjoy swimming.
mistakes.why: Enjoy is followed by a gerund.

mistakes.wrong: She is good at to cook.
mistakes.right: She is good at cooking.
mistakes.why: After a preposition, use verb-ing.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I avoid to drive at night.
I avoid driving at night.
I avoid drive at night.

exercises.prompt: She is interested in ___ pottery. (make)
___ is my favourite hobby. (Read)
Which verb is followed by a gerund?
options: finish
want
hope
He suggested to go out.

He suggested go out.

options: Do you mind to wait?
Do you mind waiting?
Do you mind wait?
a gerund used as the subject
a main verb
an adjective
assessment.why: A verb-ing used as a noun.

lessons.title: Infinitives
lessons.explain: The infinitive is to + base verb. It is used after certain verbs (want, hope, decide, plan, learn, need), after adjectives (happy to help), and to give a purpose (I went to the shop to buy milk). After modal verbs, use the base verb without to.
structures: Verb + to-infinitive: I want to learn.
Purpose: I called to ask about the price.
Adjective + to: It is easy to use.
positive: I want to improve my English.
She decided to move to Pune.
I went to the market to buy fruit.
negative: I decided not to go.
He does not want to wait.
questions: What do you want to do?
Why did you come here to study?
reallife: Plans: I hope to visit Kerala next year.
At work: I am calling to confirm our meeting.

mistakes.wrong: I want go home.
mistakes.right: I want to go home.
mistakes.why: Want is followed by to + base verb.

mistakes.wrong: I went to the shop for buy milk.
mistakes.right: I went to the shop to buy milk.
mistakes.why: Use to + base verb to show purpose.

exercises.prompt: I hope ___ you soon. (see)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: She can to swim.
She can swim.
She can swimming.
exercises.why: After a modal, use the base verb without to.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I decided not to go.
I decided to not going.
I not decided to go.

exercises.prompt: I use an app ___ learn English. (to / for)
exercises.why: To + base verb gives the purpose.

options: He wants to buy a car.
He wants buying a car.
He wants buy a car.

options: She promised to help.

She promised help.

assessment.why: After must, use the base verb.

lessons.title: Participles
lessons.explain: A participle is a verb form used as an adjective or in a verb phrase. The present participle (-ing) describes the thing that causes a feeling (a boring film). The past participle (-ed or irregular) describes the person who has the feeling (I am bored).
structures: Present participle: an interesting book, a running tap.
Past participle: a broken window, a tired child.
Feelings: -ing = causing it, -ed = feeling it.
positive: The film was exciting.
I was excited about the trip.
She picked up the broken glass.
negative: The film was not boring.
I was not surprised.
questions: Are you interested in music?
Was the story interesting?
reallife: Giving an opinion: The lesson was interesting, but I was tired.
Describing a problem: The machine is broken.

mistakes.wrong: I am boring.
mistakes.right: I am bored.
mistakes.why: I am boring means I make others bored. I am bored means I feel bored.

mistakes.wrong: The news was shocked.
mistakes.right: The news was shocking.
mistakes.why: The thing that causes the feeling takes -ing.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: The match was ___.
options: excited
exciting

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct word: I felt ___.
options: tired
tiring

exercises.prompt: The ___ window needs repair. (break)
exercises.why: A past participle used as an adjective.

options: I am very interested in history.

a sleeping baby

options: The trip was tiring.
The trip was tired.
The trip was tiredly.

lessons.title: Relative clauses
lessons.explain: A relative clause gives more information about a noun. Use who for people, which for things, that for people or things, whose for possession. A defining clause is essential to the meaning and has no commas. A non-defining clause adds extra information and uses commas.
structures: People: The man who called is my uncle.
Things: The book which I bought is great.
Possession: The girl whose bag was stolen called the police.
positive: I know a teacher who speaks five languages.
This is the phone that I bought.
My sister, who lives in Delhi, is a doctor.
negative: The shop that I like is not open.
I do not know the man who lives next door.
questions: Is this the book that you recommended?
Who is the woman who is talking to Sam?
reallife: Describing someone: She is the colleague who helped me yesterday.
Choosing: I like the one which is blue.

mistakes.wrong: The man which lives here is kind.
mistakes.right: The man who lives here is kind.
mistakes.why: Use who for people.

mistakes.wrong: The woman who her car was stolen called me.
mistakes.right: The woman whose car was stolen called me.
mistakes.why: Use whose to show possession.

exercises.prompt: The woman ___ lives next door is a nurse. (who / which)
The book ___ I read was long. (who / which)
Choose the correct sentence.
options: He is the boy whose mother is a pilot.
He is the boy who his mother is a pilot.
He is the boy which mother is a pilot.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence needs commas?
options: My brother, who lives in Dubai, is an engineer.
The man who called is here.

exercises.why: Non-defining clauses add extra information and use commas.

lessons.title: Adjective clauses
lessons.explain: An adjective clause is a clause that describes a noun, like an adjective does. Besides who, which and that, use where for places, when for times and why for reasons. You can leave out the relative pronoun when it is the object of the clause.
structures: Place: This is the town where I grew up.
Time: I remember the day when we met.
Object pronoun left out: The film (that) we saw was great.
positive: That is the cafe where we met.
I remember the year when I started school.
The reason why he left is unknown.
negative: This is not the shop where I bought it.
I do not know the reason why she is upset.
questions: Is this the place where you work?
Do you remember the day when we met?
reallife: Directions: This is the street where the bank is.
Reminiscing: I will never forget the day when I got my first job.

mistakes.wrong: This is the house where I live in.
mistakes.right: This is the house where I live. / This is the house that I live in.
mistakes.why: Where already includes the preposition in.

mistakes.wrong: The film that we saw it was good.
mistakes.right: The film that we saw was good.
mistakes.why: Do not repeat the object. The relative pronoun already stands for it.

exercises.prompt: This is the town ___ I was born. (where / who)
I remember the day ___ we first met. (when / where)
In which sentence can 'that' be left out?
options: The book that I read was good.
The man that called is here.
The dog that barked ran away.
exercises.why: That is the object of read, so it can be omitted.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: That is the room where we study.

lessons.title: Adverb clauses
lessons.explain: An adverb clause is a dependent clause that works like an adverb. It tells us when, why, how or under what condition something happens. It starts with a conjunction such as when, while, before, after, because, although, if or unless. When it comes first, put a comma after it.
structures: Time: When I arrive, I will call you.
Reason: She left early because she was ill.
Contrast / condition: Although it was cold, we went out. Unless you hurry, you will be late.
positive: After we finished, we went home.
I will wait until you come.
He passed because he studied hard.
negative: I will not go unless you come.
Although she was not tired, she went to bed.
questions: What will you do when you finish?
Will you stay if it rains?
reallife: Making plans: Before I leave, I will lock the door.
Explaining: I could not call you because my battery died.

mistakes.wrong: When I will arrive, I will call you.
mistakes.right: When I arrive, I will call you.
mistakes.why: After when, use the present simple for the future.

mistakes.wrong: Because it was raining we stayed home
mistakes.right: Because it was raining, we stayed home.
mistakes.why: Put a comma after an adverb clause at the start of a sentence.

exercises.prompt: I will call you as soon as I ___. (arrive)
exercises.why: Present simple after as soon as.

lessons.title: Noun clauses
lessons.explain: A noun clause is a group of words with its own subject and verb that does the job of a noun. It can be the subject or the object of a verb, or follow a preposition. Noun clauses often begin with that, whether, if, or a question word (what, where, when, why, how, who). In a noun clause the word order is like a statement, even after a question word: I know where she lives, not where does she live.
structures: That-clause: subject + verb + that + subject + verb: I know that he is late.
Question-word clause: subject + verb + question word + subject + verb: Tell me where you live.
If or whether clause: subject + verb + if/whether + subject + verb: I wonder if she will come.
positive: I think that she is right.
Can you tell me where the station is?
What he said surprised everyone.
I don't know whether he will come.
negative: I don't know where she lives.
He didn't say what he wanted.
I'm not sure if they have arrived.
questions: Do you know what time the shop opens?
Could you tell me how much this costs?
reallife: Asking politely: Could you tell me where the post office is?
At work: I'm not sure whether the report is ready.

mistakes.wrong: Can you tell me where is the bank?
mistakes.right: Can you tell me where the bank is?
mistakes.why: In a noun clause use statement word order: subject + verb.

mistakes.wrong: I don't know where does she live.
mistakes.right: I don't know where she lives.
mistakes.why: Do not use do, does or did in a noun clause.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.

options: I don't know why did he leave.

assessment.why: Use statement order and the past tense: why he left.

assessment.why: What she said is the subject of was.

options: She asked me where I lived.

lessons.title: Comparisons and degrees of comparison
lessons.explain: Use the comparative to compare two things and the superlative to compare three or more. Short adjectives add -er and -est (taller, tallest). Long adjectives use more and most (more expensive, most expensive). Use as ... as to say two things are equal.
structures: Comparative: taller than, more interesting than.
Superlative: the tallest, the most interesting.
Equal: as tall as, not as expensive as.
positive: Mumbai is bigger than Pune.
This is the best restaurant in town.
She is as tall as her brother.
negative: This phone is not as expensive as that one.
He is not taller than me.
questions: Which is cheaper, the red or the blue?
Who is the oldest in your family?
reallife: Shopping: This one is cheaper, but that one is better quality.
Travel: The train is faster than the bus.

mistakes.wrong: She is more taller than me.
mistakes.right: She is taller than me.
mistakes.why: Do not use more with an -er comparative.

mistakes.wrong: This is the most good book.
mistakes.right: This is the best book.
mistakes.why: Good has an irregular superlative: best.

lessons.title: Question tags
lessons.explain: A question tag is a short question added to a statement to check information or ask for agreement. After a positive statement use a negative tag. After a negative statement use a positive tag. The tag repeats the helping verb and uses a pronoun.
structures: Positive + negative tag: You are tired, aren't you?
Negative + positive tag: She doesn't smoke, does she?
No helping verb: use do/does/did: He works here, doesn't he?
positive: It is cold today, isn't it?
You like coffee, don't you?
They have left, haven't they?
negative: You are not tired, are you?
She didn't call, did she?
questions: You can swim, can't you?
We should leave now, shouldn't we?
reallife: Small talk: Lovely weather, isn't it?
Checking: The meeting is at ten, isn't it?

mistakes.wrong: You like tea, aren't you?
mistakes.right: You like tea, don't you?
mistakes.why: The tag must match the helping verb of the statement. Like uses do.

mistakes.wrong: She isn't here, isn't she?
mistakes.right: She isn't here, is she?
mistakes.why: A negative statement needs a positive tag.

You don't smoke, ___ you? (do / don't)

options: isn't she

options: haven't they
don't they
aren't they

lessons.title: Punctuation
lessons.explain: Punctuation makes writing clear. Use a full stop to end a statement, a question mark to end a question and an exclamation mark for strong feeling. Use commas in lists, after introductory phrases and before conjunctions joining two sentences. Use an apostrophe for contractions and possession.
structures: Comma in a list: I bought apples, bananas and milk.
Apostrophe: it's (it is), Maria's book (belongs to Maria).
Capital letters: names, I, the first word of a sentence.
positive: I bought apples, oranges and bananas.
Maria's brother lives in Delhi.
It's raining, so I'm staying home.
negative: I don't like coffee, but I like tea.
She isn't coming.
questions: Where's my phone?
Are you coming, or are you staying?
reallife: Writing an email: Hi Anna, thanks for your message. I'll reply tomorrow.
A note: Dad's keys are on the table.

mistakes.wrong: Its raining outside.
mistakes.right: It's raining outside.
mistakes.why: It's is short for it is.

mistakes.wrong: I have two sister's.
mistakes.right: I have two sisters.
mistakes.why: Do not use an apostrophe to make a plural.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct sentence.
options: I need eggs, milk and bread.
I need eggs milk, and bread.
I need, eggs milk and bread.
exercises.why: Commas separate items in a list.

options: the dogs bowl
the dog's bowl

options: What time is it?
